hero.title: Grounding Techniques
hero.lead:
Grounding is what you do when a feeling has gotten bigger than your ability to think about it — a panic surge, a flashback, dissociation's strange flat distance. The goal is modest: attention back in the present, body out of full alarm — the feeling becomes something you ride out, not something that carries you off.

The techniques below are sorted by distress level — it decides what works. A gentle noticing exercise is excellent at a four out of ten and useless at a nine — not user error; a nine means your thinking brain isn't available. Pick from the right shelf.

sections.heading: What grounding is — and what it isn't
sections.html:
Grounding is a distress tolerance skill: it gets you through the next fifteen minutes without making anything worse. It doesn't solve the problem or process the memory — expecting that is how it gets written off. It isn't distraction but its opposite: attention put somewhere specific and physical, right now. And it isn't relaxation — you may still feel awful afterwards. The win is feeling awful and present, able to decide what's next.

Practicing on a calm Tuesday feels pointless, and it's exactly what makes a technique available at a bad Saturday's nine. Calm-day practice is the actual training.

sections.heading: Techniques by intensity
sections.html:
As distress rises, what works gets more physical and less cognitive; above about an eight, only techniques that change body chemistry still land.

IntensityWhat it feels likeTechniques that work
Mild (1–3)Uneasy, tense, mind drifting to worries5-4-3-2-1; naming what you see out loud; a warm drink in both hands; bare feet on the floor
Moderate (4–6)Clearly anxious, racing thoughts, restlessnessPaced breathing; a walk with attention on your footfall; naming ten cities; an ice cube; stretching shoulders and jaw
High (7–8)Trembling, chest tight, thinking has narrowedCold water on face or wrists; bilateral movement — walking, alternating taps; a strong sour or minty taste; pushing hard against a wall
Crisis (9–10)Panic, dissociation, urges you don't want to act onCold pack over the eyes and cheeks; a short burst of intense exercise; slow paced breathing; then contact a person — a friend, a helpline, your therapist's out-of-hours number

The higher rows are the DBT distress tolerance module's TIPP skills. Health note: cold water and intense exercise deliberately change your heart rate — check with your doctor first if you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, are pregnant, or take medication affecting your heart rate. Breathing and sensory techniques suit almost everyone.

sections.heading: The four core techniques, properly
sections.html:
5-4-3-2-1

Usually taught too fast. Slowly name five things you can see, four you can feel, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste — specific ("the scratch on the arm of the blue chair", not "a chair") and out loud — speaking recruits more attention than thinking.

Temperature

The fastest-acting. Cold water on the face, or a cold pack over the eyes and cheeks while you breathe out slowly, triggers the dive reflex and slows the heart within seconds.

Paced breathing

An out-breath longer than the in-breath engages the calming branch of the nervous system: in for four, out for six, kept comfortable; forcing it can leave you lightheaded. Five or six cycles is enough — nobody in the meeting will know.

Bilateral movement

Anything rhythmically alternating left and right: walking, especially outside; alternating taps; an object passed hand to hand. It seems to settle a fear response — why a walk so often beats an hour of trying to think your way out.

sections.heading: What to do afterwards
sections.html:
When grounding works, you're not fine — you're present, shaky, and tired. Treat the next hour as recovery:

  1. Warmth, something to eat or drink, and company if you have it. Blood sugar and temperature take a hit, and another person is itself regulating.
  2. Lower the demands for an hour — a second surge is far likelier walking straight back into what triggered the first.
  3. Write down three things while fresh: how high it got, what preceded it, what you tried and whether it helped.
  4. Skip the post-mortem. Analysis straight afterwards usually turns into rumination; save it for a calm day, ideally with your therapist.

The third step compounds: a few weeks of it produces a ranked list worth more than any article — this one included. The trigger column feeds into tracking anxiety.

sections.heading: Keeping a list: paper vs an app
sections.html:
Two needs: the techniques written where you'll find them in a bad moment, and a record of which worked. An index card in your wallet does the first beautifully — no battery, no unlocking, no notifications.

Paper struggles with the second job: loose cards never add up to an answer. The app handles it — five seconds to log a moment, a note for which technique helped, charts of how often spikes happen and what rides along, widgets and reminders, and PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON export for the therapist who asks. Private by default: iCloud sync, no account, no email.

Feeltracker Mood & BPD won't talk you down — that's what the techniques above are for. It remembers, honestly, which of them worked, so next time you choose from your own list, not a generic one.

items.question: Why doesn't 5-4-3-2-1 work for me?
items.answer: Most often it's being used at the wrong intensity. Sensory noticing needs working attention, and above roughly a seven out of ten that attention isn't available. Try a physical technique instead — cold water, paced breathing, movement — and save 5-4-3-2-1 for earlier in the climb.

items.question: How long should grounding take to work?
items.answer: Temperature and paced breathing often shift something within a minute or two; sensory and movement techniques take five to ten. If nothing has moved after about fifteen minutes, switch technique rather than trying harder at the same one — and if you're in real crisis, reach out to a person or a crisis line rather than continuing alone.

items.question: Can grounding help with dissociation?
items.answer: It's one of the main uses. When you feel unreal or detached, physical techniques tend to work best: cold, strong tastes, texture under your fingers, feet firmly on the floor, naming objects out loud. If dissociation is frequent, raise it with a professional — it often has a history behind it that deserves proper support.

items.question: Should I practice when I'm calm?
items.answer: Yes — it's the single biggest thing that makes grounding work when it counts. A technique you've run through on an ordinary day is available automatically; one you've only read about has to be learned in the worst possible conditions. Two minutes a few times a week is plenty.

items.question: Is grounding a substitute for therapy?
items.answer: No. Grounding gets you through the moment; it doesn't address what's generating the moments. It works best alongside proper support — see [DBT skills](/mood-journal/dbt-skills/) for the framework these techniques come from, and speak to a doctor or therapist if you're needing them often.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Grounding techniques help you get through difficult moments; they do not treat an underlying condition, and needing them often is a good reason to speak with a doctor or therapist. Check with your doctor before using the cold-water or intense-exercise techniques if you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, are pregnant, or take medication that affects your heart rate. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself or of suicide, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line in your country right away — that is what they are there for.
